disclaimer: MODELED interpretation of a CALCULATED ranking grounded in OBSERVED claims. Not a forecast and not investment advice. Areas worth investigating, not securities to buy.
current_reality: The ranking does not say AI datacenters lack capital, chips, or announced campuses. It says energization is gated by long-lead high-voltage equipment. Large power transformers score #1 because they sit on both the grid path and the behind-the-meter generation path, substitution is poor, and 2026 OEM filings show transformer-driven order growth with book-to-bill still above 1. Microsoft’s primary testimony is that GPUs were waiting on space or power — not the reverse. Confidence stays moderate because 2026 week-level lead times are still secondary (GAO’s 18–36 month finding is 2023).
constraint_migration: The engine relieves transformer capacity/lead-time/concentration only, then re-ranks. Grid interconnection rises next: study queues and post-agreement upgrades still take years even if a transformer slot appears. Heavy-duty gas turbines are close behind as the main substitute for slow grid power — and they still need GSU transformers, so turbine relief does not fully bypass this node.
gains_leverage: LPT/GSU manufacturers and the electrical-steel / specialized plant capacity behind them (Siemens Energy Grid Technologies, Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova Electrification)
ISO/RTO interconnection throughput and utilities that can actually construct assigned upgrades after an ISA
Behind-the-meter / dedicated generation packages only after GSU delivery is credible — GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Power as slot holders, not as a free substitute
Switchgear and campus electrical distribution (Eaton-class) as complementary gear, not as the same scarcity as LPTs
loses_leverage: The story that GPU scarcity is what currently stops GW-scale halls from turning on
Queue-reform narratives that treat a faster study as equivalent to an energized campus
2030 OEM expansion announcements treated as 2026 deliverable capacity
Cooling and shell construction as the system bottleneck — demand is real; the evidence does not show they bind first
second_order_effect: Clearing transformers does not create megawatts. LBNL shows 549 GW already holding an interconnection agreement and not operating. GE Vernova’s >$5B year-to-date datacenter orders are Electrification (grid gear), not Gas Power — so AI demand is already pulling the transformer/switchgear stack harder than the turbine book, of which only a minority is datacenter. The coupled trap: the substitute for slow interconnection (new gas) still consumes the same constrained GSU transformers.
opportunity: Worth investigating: who can actually deliver LPTs/GSUs into 2027–2028 AI interconnects; surplus-interconnection or co-location that avoids a new substation; whether switchgear stays a demand boom or becomes a second equipment queue; and which generation projects have both a turbine slot and a GSU. Not a conclusion: utilities-in-general or turbines-as-grid-replacement.

confirm: OEM transformer book-to-bill remains well above 1.0 while data-center projects remain in Electrification order commentary
Primary 2026 LPT/GSU lead-time disclosures stay multi-year (not just 2023 GAO or secondary surveys)
LBNL IA-not-COD backlog stays large even as study reforms are claimed
Hyperscalers continue to describe power/space, not chips, as the bind
invalidate: Major LPT OEMs report book-to-bill near 1.0 and returning 12–18 month quotes
Primary datacenter load-queue data show study time — not equipment — as the remaining clock
Hyperscalers report idle energized halls waiting on GPUs
New generation reaches COD fast enough in AI zones that transformer scarcity no longer gates energization

confidence.rationale: Matches transformer-node evidence confidence. Direction (optics of power-delivery over chips; cascade into interconnection then turbines) is better supported than the exact #1 margin over interconnection. Load vs generation queue distinction remains a material caveat.
